> My guess is that if you can alter this one key then it might lead to widespread compromise whereas if you just modify someone's password that just affects their account.

AFAIU, we are talking a per user (actually, per user authentication device) <del>secret</del> public key, are we not?

> My guess is that if you can alter this one key then it might lead to widespread compromise whereas if you just modify someone's password that just affects their account.

AFAIU, we are talking a per user (actually, per user authentication device) secret, are we not?

Here is the [wording for *verifiers*](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html#sfcv) in the NIST sp800-63b draft:

> The verifier has either a symmetric or an asymmetric public cryptographic key that corresponds to each authenticator. While <mark>both types of keys SHALL be protected against modification, symmetric keys SHALL additionally be protected against unauthorized disclosure by access controls</mark> that limit access to the key to only those software components that require access

Here is the [wording for *authenticators*](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html#sfca):

> The key SHOULD be stored in appropriate storage available to the authenticator (e.g., <mark>keychain storage</mark>), or <mark>if the key is to be non-exportable, it SHALL be stored in an isolated execution environment protected by hardware</mark> or in a separate processor with a controlled interface to the central processing unit of the user endpoint.

For *authenticators*, they recommend (but do *not* require) using HSM or similar.

However, they don't have this requirement for *verifiers*, they only say that there must be some protection against unauthorized disclosure and modification. I understand, that access control is considered to be OK.
